text.p: Austrian markets rallied on Monday after Finance Minister Viktor Klima emerged as successor to outgoing Chancellor Franz Vranitzky but analysts said the vacancy at the treasury may prove more difficult to fill.
Chancellor Vranitzky announced his resignation on Saturday and Social Democratic Party leaders swiftly installed Viktor Klima as government and party head.
The blue-chip ATX index jumped 0.8 percent to a high of 1,175.53 on Monday before easing back slightly.
Austrian government bond futures were up 20 basis points in March at 108.40.

"Admittedly, one does not normally associate resignations with stability but there is no doubt that this particular change will contribute to stability in Austria," said Roland Neuwirth, an analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Vienna.

The timing of Vranitzky's departure was impeccable, Neuwirth said. Klima had inherited a Social Democratic Party strengthened within the two-party coalition after it won a privatisation battle over Creditanstalt bank a week ago.
"Vranitzky chose his moment perfectly. Politically things had quietened down...and Klima's popularity ratings are excellent," Neuwirth said.

Investors and analysts were unanimous in their positive assessment of Klima's political abilities. As finance minister he negotiated a tough two-year budget with coalition partner the conservative People's Party and lay the groundwork for Austrian participation in a single European currency.
"At least we'll be getting a chancellor who knows something about the economy," a Vienna share trader said.

Tempering the market's upbeat assessment of Chancellor Klima, however, was a question mark hanging over who would take on the key job of finance minister and attempt to guide Austria into European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Among the new finance minister's first tasks will be the drawing up of the 1998 and 1999 budgets. Talks with the People's Party are due to start in March.

"It is difficult to come up with someone who is a heavyweight in both political and financial terms. They need someone with a long experience within the business community who is also a political heavyweight," said Alfred Reisenberger, analyst at IMI Sigeco in London.

Faced with the lack of an obvious candidate within the government, Austrian media have widened their search to take in leading financial and industrial figures and politicians outside the top echelon.

Max Kothbauer, Creditanstalt deputy chief and former top aid to Vranitzky, was among the most popular choices. Othmar Puehrinher, chief executive of engineering group VA Technologie AG, also figured along with Erich Becker, chief financial officer of state holding company OeIAG.
State secretary for civil servants Karl Schloegl was among the political front runners.
"It's always a risk to bring in someone from outside. They must also possess the political know-how," said Neuwirth.
Klima's predecessor, Andreas Staribacher was the last outsider to take on the finance portfolio. He survived only eight months in the job.
